chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: Every construction uses only an unmarked ruler and a compass, and every one is followed by its reason: which triangles are congruent, and by which condition. The chapter opens with a pair of eyes drawn with two arcs and ends with tilings, where counting and colouring decide what is possible.

points.title: Try first, name later
points.text: The hook video leaves the eyes question open: where must the compass point go so that both arcs meet at the corners? The perpendicular bisector is named only after the student has found the two centres.

points.title: Every step has a reason
points.text: Each construction is justified by congruent triangles: SSS for the bisector, the copied angle and the angle bisector, SAS for the right angle at the midpoint, and an equilateral triangle for 60°.

points.text: Each idea gets its own topic: one video per concept, a closing practice concept (with a tool where the manipulation is the idea), then the book's Figure it Out questions in their own topic, one question and one video per concept.

concepts.concept_name: Two arcs make an eye

content.text:
6 Constructions and Tilings
6.1 Geometric Constructions
Eyes
Do you recall the 'Eyes' construction we did in Grade 6?
Of course, eyes can be drawn freehand, but we wanted to construct them so that the lower arc and upper arc of each eye look symmetrical. We relied on our spatial estimation to determine the two centres, A and B (see the figure), from which we drew the lower arc and upper arc respectively.
The arcs define a line XY that 'supports' the drawing though it is not part of the final figure. We can start with this supporting line and systematically find the centres A and B.

concepts.concept_name: Finding the centres A and B

content.text:
For the eye to be symmetrical, or for the supporting line to be the line of symmetry, the upper and lower arcs should have the same radius. In other words, we must have AX = BX. Since AX = AY and BX = BY, this means AX = AY = BX = BY.
How do we find such A and B?
From X and Y, draw arcs above and below XY, with the same radii. The two points at which the arcs meet, above and below XY, give us A and B, respectively.
Use this to construct an eye.
Join A and B with a line. Where does AB intersect XY, and what is the angle formed between them?
We observe that AB passes through the midpoint of XY, and is also perpendicular to it.
A division of a line, or any geometrical object, into two identical parts is called bisection. A line that bisects a given line and is perpendicular to it, is called the perpendicular bisector.

content.text:
Worked example: XY is a line segment. Using only a ruler and a compass, find the centres A and B for the two arcs of an eye with corners X and Y, and draw the eye.
1. Open the compass to a radius more than half of XY.
2. With centre X, draw an arc above XY and an arc below XY.
3. With centre Y and the same radius, draw arcs that cut the first two arcs.
4. Name the meeting point above XY as A and the one below XY as B. Then AX = AY = BX = BY.
5. With centre A and radius AX, draw the lower arc from X to Y.
6. With centre B and the same radius, draw the upper arc from X to Y. The two arcs make the eye.
Answer: A and B are the meeting points of equal arcs from X and Y; the arc centred at A is the lower arc and the arc centred at B is the upper arc

concepts.concept_name: Why AB is the perpendicular bisector

content.text:
Will the line joining the two points at which the arcs meet, above and below XY, always be the perpendicular bisector of XY, i.e., when XY is of any length, and the arcs are drawn using a radius of any length?
This can be answered through congruence. Let us consider a line segment XY. Find points A and B such that AX = AY = BX = BY. Draw the lines AB, AX, AY, BX and BY. Let O be the point of intersection between AB and XY.
Which two triangles should be congruent for AB to be the perpendicular bisector of XY (that is, O is the midpoint of XY and AB is perpendicular to XY)?
If we show that ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY, then OX = OY, and ∠AOX = ∠AOY because they are corresponding parts of congruent triangles. Since ∠AOX and ∠AOY together form a straight angle, we have ∠AOX + ∠AOY = 180°. Thus, ∠AOX = ∠AOY = 90°. This establishes that O is the midpoint of XY and AB is perpendicular to XY.
In ΔAOX and ΔAOY, we already know that AX = AY, and AO is common to both triangles.
If we can show that ∠XAO = ∠YAO then, by the SAS congruence condition, we can conclude that the triangles are congruent.
To show this, we observe that ΔABX ≅ ΔABY. This is so because AX = AY, BX = BY, and AB is common to both the triangles.
Thus, we have ∠XAB = ∠YAB, or ∠XAO = ∠YAO because they are corresponding parts of congruent triangles.
Hence, AB is the perpendicular bisector of XY.

concepts.concept_name: Every point equally far from X and Y lies on AB

content.text:
We can have eyes of different shapes. How do we get these different shapes? Try!
One way is to choose two other points C and D such that CX = CY = DX = DY. An eye of a different shape can be drawn using these points.
Will C and D lie on the perpendicular bisector AB?
The points C and D are at the same distance from both X and Y. We have just seen that joining any two such points gives the perpendicular bisector of XY. Since XY has only one perpendicular bisector, which is the line AB, the points C and D must lie on the line AB.
Justify the following statement using the facts that we have established. Any point that has the same distance from X and Y lies on the perpendicular bisector of XY.
Thus, eyes of different shapes can be drawn by suitably choosing different pairs of points on the perpendicular bisector as centres to construct the upper and lower arcs of the eyes.

maths_rules: Given AX = AY and BX = BY; AB is common to triangles ABX and ABY, so triangle ABX is congruent to triangle ABY by SSS.
Corresponding parts are equal, so angle XAB = angle YAB, that is angle XAO = angle YAO, because O lies on AB.
In triangles AOX and AOY: AX = AY, angle XAO = angle YAO, AO is common, so they are congruent by SAS.
So OX = OY (O is the midpoint of XY) and angle AOX = angle AOY.
Angle AOX + angle AOY = 180 degrees (straight angle), and the two are equal, so each is 180 / 2 = 90 degrees.
video_script.design: One idea: two congruences in a chain. Triangles ABX and ABY by SSS give the equal angles at A. Triangles AOX and AOY by SAS give the midpoint and the right angles. Keeko's doubt is that looking alike is enough.

concepts.concept_name: Steps to construct the perpendicular bisector

content.text:
Construction of Perpendicular Bisector
Given a line segment XY, how do we draw its perpendicular bisector using only an unmarked ruler and a compass?
We have seen that joining any two points, one above XY and one below, that are at equal distances from X and Y, gives the perpendicular bisector of XY. This gives a method to construct the perpendicular bisector.
1. Taking some fixed radius, from X and then Y, construct two sufficiently long arcs above XY. Name the point where the arcs meet as A.
2. Using the same radius, from X and then Y, construct two sufficiently long arcs below XY. Name the point where the arcs meet as B.
3. AB is the required perpendicular bisector.
Thus, the perpendicular bisector can be constructed using the simplest geometric tools, an unmarked ruler and a compass. We will use only these two tools for all the other geometric constructions in this chapter, unless there is a need for drawing lines of specific lengths in standard units.
This method of constructing the perpendicular bisector is not only geometrically exact but also a practical way to construct it accurately.
This method to find the midpoint of a line segment is more accurate than measuring the length using a marked scale.

content.text:
Worked example: Draw a line segment XY. Construct its perpendicular bisector using only an unmarked ruler and a compass, and mark the midpoint of XY.
1. Open the compass to a radius more than half of XY, so that the arcs will meet.
2. With centre X, draw a long arc above XY. With centre Y and the same radius, draw an arc above XY that cuts it. Name the meeting point A.
3. Keep the same radius. With centres X and Y, draw two arcs below XY that cut each other at B.
4. Join A and B with the ruler. AB is the perpendicular bisector of XY.
5. Mark O where AB crosses XY. O is the midpoint of XY, and ∠AOX = 90°.
6. Reason: AX = AY and BX = BY, so ΔABX ≅ ΔABY by SSS and then ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SAS.
Answer: AB, the line through the two meeting points of equal arcs, is the perpendicular bisector; it meets XY at its midpoint O

content.text:
Construction of a 90° Angle at a Given Point
Can we extend the method of constructing the perpendicular bisector to construct a 90° angle at any point on a line? Draw a line and mark a point O on it. Construct a 90° angle at point O.
Find a segment of this line for which O is the midpoint.
Extend the line on either side of O. Using a compass, mark two points X and Y at equal distance from O, so that O is the midpoint of XY.
The perpendicular bisector of XY will pass through O and is perpendicular to the given line.
In this case, do we need to draw two pairs of intersecting arcs to get the perpendicular bisector of XY?
No, we don't. We already have one point, O, lying on the perpendicular bisector.

content.text:
Worked example: Draw a line and mark a point O on it. Construct a 90° angle at O using only a ruler and a compass, and say why the angle is 90°.
1. With centre O and any radius, draw arcs that cut the line at X and at Y. Then OX = OY.
2. Open the compass wider than OX. With centre X, draw an arc above the line.
3. With centre Y and the same radius, draw an arc that cuts it at A. Then AX = AY.
4. Join O and A. ∠AOX is the required 90° angle.
5. Reason: in ΔAOX and ΔAOY, AX = AY, OX = OY, and AO is common, so ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SSS.
6. So ∠AOX = ∠AOY. Together they make 180°, so each is 90°.
Answer: ∠AOX = 90°, since ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SSS and the two equal angles make a straight angle

concepts.concept_name: Steps to bisect an angle, and why they work

content.text:
We will now develop a general method to bisect any angle. Consider an angle ∠XOY.
We can bisect it if we can draw two congruent triangles ΔOBC and ΔOAC as shown in the figure. Then ∠BOC = ∠AOC.
How do we construct these congruent triangles, given the angle?
If A and B are marked such that OA = OB, and if C is chosen such that BC = AC, then by the SSS congruence condition, ΔOBC ≅ ΔOAC. So we can bisect an angle as follows.
Steps for Angle Bisection
1. Mark points A and B such that OA = OB.
2. Choosing any sufficiently long radius, cut arcs from A and B, keeping the radius same. Mark the point of intersection as C.
3. OC bisects ∠AOB.

Worked example: Draw any angle ∠XOY. Bisect it using only a ruler and a compass, and justify that the two parts are equal.
1. With centre O and any radius, draw an arc that cuts OY at A and OX at B. Then OA = OB.
2. With centre A and a radius long enough for the arcs to meet, draw an arc inside the angle.
3. With centre B and the same radius, draw an arc that cuts it at C. Then AC = BC.
4. Join O and C.
5. In ΔOAC and ΔOBC: OA = OB, AC = BC, and OC is common. So ΔOAC ≅ ΔOBC by SSS.
6. So ∠AOC = ∠BOC, and OC bisects ∠XOY.

concepts.concept_name: A 45° angle and the eight-petal design

content.text:
Angle Bisection for a Design
How do we construct this figure? (Eight equal petals meet at one centre.)
The supporting lines for this figure will look like this.
What is the angle between two adjacent lines?
We need the angle between every pair of adjacent lines to be equal. Since 360° is equally divided into 8 parts, every angle is 45°.
How do we construct a 45° angle using only a ruler and a compass?
We know how to construct a 90° angle. If we can divide it into two equal parts, or bisect it, then we get a 45° angle.
So, a 45° angle can be constructed by first constructing a 90° angle and then bisecting it.

content.text:
Worked example: Eight equal petals meet at a centre, along eight equally spaced supporting lines. Find the angle between neighbouring lines, and construct it with a ruler and a compass.
1. The eight angles round the centre are equal and make a full turn of 360°.
2. The full turn of 360° shared by 8 equal angles gives 45° each.
3. Draw a line and mark the centre O on it. Construct a 90° angle at O with equal arcs.
4. Bisect the 90° angle: arcs from O cut the two arms at A and B, then equal arcs from A and B meet at C. OC makes 45° with each arm (SSS).
5. Extend the two arms and the bisector through O, and bisect one more right angle; this gives four lines, which is eight half-lines from O at 45° to each other.
Answer: Each angle is 45°; construct 90° and bisect it

maths_rules: An arc with centre O cuts OY at A and OX at B: OA = OB.
Arcs of one radius from A and from B, long enough to meet inside the angle, meet at C: AC = BC.
In triangles OAC and OBC: OA = OB, AC = BC, OC common, so triangle OAC is congruent to triangle OBC by SSS.

media.context: Constructions and Tilings. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Eight equal petals meet at a centre along eight equally spaced lines. maths_rules: Eight equal angles round the centre make a full turn of 360 degrees.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (angle bisection), Q1

content.text:
Figure it Out (angle bisection), Q1: Construct at least 4 different angles. Draw their bisectors.
1. Draw four angles of clearly different sizes, for example a small acute angle, a right angle made with equal arcs, a large acute angle and an obtuse angle.
2. For each angle with vertex O: with centre O draw an arc that cuts the arms at A and B, so OA = OB.
3. With one radius, draw arcs from A and from B that meet at C inside the angle.
4. Join OC. It is the bisector, because ΔOAC ≅ ΔOBC by SSS.
5. Check: fold the paper along OC; the two arms land on each other.
Answer: Each bisector is OC, where OA = OB and AC = BC; ΔOAC ≅ ΔOBC by SSS, so the two halves are equal

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (angle bisection), Q3

content.text:
Figure it Out (angle bisection), Q3: In Step 2 of angle bisection, if arcs of equal radius are drawn on the other side, so that the arcs from A and B meet at a point C on the far side of the vertex O, outside the angle, will the line OC still be an angle bisector? Explore this through construction, and then justify your answer.
1. Mark A and B on the arms with OA = OB.
2. With a radius larger than OA, draw equal arcs from A and B on the far side of O; they meet at C, with AC = BC.
3. In ΔOAC and ΔOBC: OA = OB, AC = BC, and OC is common.
4. So ΔOAC ≅ ΔOBC by SSS, and ∠AOC = ∠BOC.
5. Extend CO beyond O to a point D inside ∠AOB. ∠AOD and ∠AOC make a straight angle, and so do ∠BOD and ∠BOC.
6. So ∠AOD = 180° − ∠AOC and ∠BOD = 180° − ∠BOC; these are equal, so the line CO, extended beyond O, bisects ∠AOB.
Answer: Yes. OA = OB, AC = BC and OC is common, so ΔOAC ≅ ΔOBC by SSS and ∠AOC = ∠BOC; their supplements are equal too, so the line CO, extended beyond O, still bisects ∠AOB

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (angle bisection), Q4

content.text:
Figure it Out (angle bisection), Q4: What are the other angles that can be constructed using angle bisection? Can you construct 65.5° angle?
1. From 180° by halving: 90°. From 90° by halving: 45°, 22.5°, and so on.
2. Sums of these also work, for example 90° + 45° = 135° and 45° + 22.5° = 67.5°.
3. Every angle made this way, doubled enough times, becomes a whole multiple of 45°.
4. 65.5° doubled is 131°, and every further doubling is 131° times a power of 2, which is never a multiple of 45°, because 131 is not divisible by 3 or by 5.
5. So 65.5° cannot be constructed by bisection.
6. Later in this chapter we build a 60° angle; halving it gives 30° and 15°, and sums such as 75°. Those all double into multiples of 15°, and 131° times a power of 2 is not one of them either.
Answer: Angles such as 90°, 45°, 22.5°, 135° and 67.5° can be made (and, once 60° is built, 30°, 15° and 75°); 65.5° cannot, because no number of doublings turns it into a multiple of 45°, or even of 15°

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (angle bisection), Q6

content.text:
Figure it Out (angle bisection), Q6: Construct the following figure: a square with four equal petals inside it, each petal running from the centre of the square to one corner. How do we construct the petals so that they are of the maximum possible size within a given square?
1. Construct a square: a segment, right angles at both ends, equal sides cut with the compass, and join the fourth side.
2. Find the midpoint of each side by constructing its perpendicular bisector.
3. The two bisectors through opposite midpoints cross at the centre of the square.
4. With centre the midpoint of one side and radius half the side, draw a semicircle inside the square. It passes through the two corners at the ends of that side and through the centre.
5. Do the same from the other three midpoints. Each petal is where two semicircles overlap, from the centre to a corner.
6. These arcs just touch the sides of the square at the corners, so the petals are as large as they can be.
Answer: Find the midpoints of the four sides; from each midpoint draw a semicircle of radius half the side inside the square; the four petals run from the centre to the corners and are the largest possible

maths_rules: Adding two built angles: 90 + 45 = 135, 45 + 22.5 = 67.5.

maths_rules: Square ABCD: right angles at A and B by equal arcs, AD = BC = AB cut with the compass, and D joined to C.
Midpoints P, Q, R, S of AB, BC, CD, DA by perpendicular bisectors; the bisectors through P and R and through Q and S cross at the centre O.
PO = half of AB, because P is the midpoint of AB and PO is perpendicular to AB with O at half the height. PA = PB = half of AB too.
A semicircle with centre P and radius PA, inside the square, passes through A, B and O. The same holds for Q, R and S.
Two neighbouring semicircles, for example from P and from Q, overlap in a petal from O to B. Four such petals run from O to A, B, C and D.
A radius longer than half the side from P would cut the sides of the square beyond the corners, so the arc leaves the square.

content.text:
Repeating Units and Repeating Angles
Consider a design made of a row of five equal sectors (shapes with two equal straight arms and an arc), alternately pointing down and up, with neighbouring sectors sharing an arm. In this design, there is a single unit repeating itself. To construct this figure, we need to make exact copies of this unit in two different orientations.
In order to make exact copies, all the units must have the same arm lengths and the same angle between the arms. We can ensure equal arm lengths using a compass, but how do we ensure equal angles?
Let us develop a method to create an exact copy of a given angle.
Draw an angle. Create a copy of this angle using only a ruler and compass.
Steps of Construction to Copy an Angle
Draw an arc from A. This gives us three points that form the isosceles triangle ΔABC.
Draw an arc of the same radius from X.
Measure BC using a compass. Transfer this length on the arc from Z to get YZ = BC.
By the SSS congruence condition, ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ. So, ∠A = ∠X.

content.text:
Worked example: An angle with vertex A is drawn. Copy it onto a ray from a point X using only a ruler and a compass, and justify that the copy is equal.
1. With centre A and any radius, draw an arc that cuts the two arms at B and C. Then AB = AC.
2. Draw a ray from X. With centre X and the same radius, draw a long arc that cuts the ray at Z. Then XZ = AB.
3. Open the compass to the length BC.
4. With centre Z and radius BC, cut the arc at Y. Then YZ = BC and XY = AC.
5. Join X and Y.
6. In ΔABC and ΔXYZ: AB = XZ, AC = XY, BC = ZY. So ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ by SSS, and ∠YXZ = ∠CAB.
Answer: ∠YXZ is a copy of ∠A, because ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ by SSS

content.text:
Figure it Out (copying an angle), Q1: Construct at least 4 different angles in different orientations without taking any measurement. Make a copy of all these angles.
1. Draw four angles with the ruler only, each in a different direction on the page, for example one opening upwards, one sideways, one downwards and one slanting.
2. For each angle with vertex A: draw an arc from A cutting the arms at B and C.
3. Draw a new ray from a point X, and with the same radius draw an arc from X cutting it at Z.
4. Open the compass to BC, and from Z cut the arc at Y. Join XY.
5. Each copy is equal because ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ by SSS. Check by laying tracing paper over both.
Answer: For each angle, equal arcs from A and X and the chord BC moved to ZY give ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ by SSS, so every copy equals its angle
